answers.feedback: This is a shocking reversal of your positions, but this can help you gather even more votes in the North.

answers.description: We will bomb the shit out of 'em. I will unleash every ounce of firepower we've been holding back. Carpet bombing of Communist positions, no more restrictions on our commanders, and a naval blockade so tight nothing gets in or out. When the Reds understand that we are not leaving until they die or surrender, they will crack.
answers.feedback: This is a hawkish answer that will motivate your base.

answers.description: The problem is the politicians in Washington who think they can run a war from a desk. I'll let General Westmoreland and the men in the field make the calls. They know the terrain, they know the enemy, and they don't need Lyndon Johnson or Colonel Sanders second‑guessing every move from the White House. Give the military what they need, give them clear objectives, and then get out of their way. That's how you win.
answers.feedback: A boring and uncontroversial answer.

questions.description: In Chicago, your supporters clashed with shoutniks and beatniks on the auditorium steps. In Indiana, a violent scuffle broke out between your people and civil rights marchers. In Ohio, a chair was hurled into the crowd, leaving a dozen bloodied. The newspapers are branding your tour a 'traveling circus of lawlessness,' with some editorials calling your rallies 'flashpoints of civil disorder.' Consequently, suburban moderates are growing concerned about the optics.

answers.description: My supporters are defending themselves. They come to hear a speech, and they're met by screaming mobs who want to shut them up. The shoutniks show up looking for a fight, and when they get one, they cry to the newspapers.
answers.feedback: This really undermines your message on law and order.

answers.description: I don't want anyone getting hurt at my rallies, and I've told my people as much. But the folks who come to protest need to understand that when you scream in a man's face and shove him around, things are going to get heated.
answers.feedback: This is a good middle-ground answer but your numbers keep falling.

answers.description: This is exactly what I've been warning about. The country is coming apart because Lying Lyndon has let the radicals run wild. When I'm President, we won't have brawls in the streets because the troublemakers will know there's a price to pay!
answers.feedback: Good try, but your attempt to spin this as a law and order issue hasn't gained much traction. Your numbers keep falling.

questions.description: Colonel Sanders is leading in the polls, and you're fighting a two‑front war against him and President Johnson. Your aide Asa Carter says that you need a clear line of attack against the Colonel, something that sticks. How will you attack him?

answers.description: Hit him on civil rights. When he’s up North, he’s more than happy to march lockstep with those radical street-agitators. But the second he flies down here to the South, he tries to whisper nonsense about 'state solutions' to our people.
answers.feedback: Sanders has no answer to this; it is a solid attack if you want to sweep the South.

answers.description: Harland Sanders ain’t a southerner at all! Not only was he born in Indiana, but he once served as the Secretary to the Chamber of Commerce of Columbus, Indiana! If you believe Sanders isn’t just faking being a Southerner, then I’ve got some beachfront property in Idaho to sell ya.
answers.feedback: He’s lived in Alabama, worked in Tennessee, and is a Kentuckian. He is not far from the South.

answers.description: Sanders is a distraction. Lyndon Johnson is the man who signed the Civil Rights Act, who opened the borders, who's let our boys die in Cuba with no plan to win. The Colonel's just the Republican stand‑in. My fight is with the President.
answers.feedback: Fair.

questions.description: Your campaign started as a reaction to President Johnson's supposed betrayal of the South on issues such as civil rights and immigration. But as the campaign went on, LBJ seemed to have left the South to you and Sanders, focusing on the Midwest and Northwest instead. Will you keep attacking the President?

answers.description: They call him 'Lying Lyndon' for a reason. He promised the Cuban War would be over by Christmas 1963. It wasn't. He promised no wider war in Indochina, then doubled the troops. He said the economy was sound, then the salad oil scandal nearly sank the whole country. The man can't tell the truth if his life depended on it!
answers.feedback: "An Honest Nation Needs an Honest President. Dump Lying Lyndon!"

answers.description: Traitor Lyndon opened our borders to a flood of Cuban aliens who are taking jobs from Americans. He says he's for the working man, but the working man is worse off today than he was four years ago. I'll tell every autoworker in Michigan and every steelworker in Pennsylvania that the President sold them out while he was shaking hands with bankers and giving handouts to foreigners.
answers.feedback: That's a message that could resonate in the industrial North where you're trying to grow.

answers.description: Frankly, Lyndon Johnson is a distraction. He's a lame duck who lost his own party months ago. My real opponent in this race is Colonel Sanders
answers.feedback: Fair.

questions.description: A Cam bomb struck the U.S. Embassy in Havana, seriously wounding the American ambassador. Two days later, an explosive report surfaced: American troops may have massacred at least 90 unarmed Vietnamese civilians near the Laos border. The President is getting massacred in the polls, as voters are coming to trust Sanders instead.

answers.description: Lying Lyndon strikes again.

questions.description: As a result of the ongoing Cuban war, every week brings another boatload of Cubans to Florida's shores. As governor, you claimed that they're filling up shelters, taking low-wage jobs, and straining Florida's hospitals and schools. Now you're running for President, and the crisis is worse than ever. What exactly will you do about the flood of refugees?

answers.description: I'll stop the boats before they reach our shores. The Navy and Coast Guard will turn back every vessel carrying aliens. No exceptions. As for the ones already here, they can pack their bags and go home.
answers.feedback: "America First! America First!" the crowd cheers.

answers.description: First, we seal the border. Nobody else gets in without proper vetting, and anyone with ties to Castro's leftovers is turned away on the spot. Second, we prioritize American jobs. Refugees with skills we actually need can stay and work, provided they follow the law. The rest can find some other country to take them.
answers.feedback: This is a more moderate position compared to your earlier stance, but why? Your core supporters are confused.

answers.description: These refugees are fleeing the very Communists I've promised to crush. Some of them are good people. The genuine ones can stay until Cuba is safe again.
answers.feedback: This is too liberal for you, and you will lose votes.

questions.description: Your advisor Asa Carter is staring at the electoral map spread across the table. 'Governor,' he says, 'we've got the Deep South locked, including Alabama, Mississippi, South Carolina and Florida. But we're polling in the single digits everywhere else, and states like Arkansas, Louisiana, North Carolina are also toss-ups. Are we trying to pull off an upset and win this thing outright, or are we playing for a deadlock and a seat at the bargaining table in Congress?'

answers.description: I didn't get into this race to be a spoiler. Johnson is bleeding support, Sanders is a fad that'll fade, and if we can pick off a few border states and hold what we've got, I'll have a path to 270. Don't tell me about deadlocks. Tell me how we get to a majority.
answers.feedback: Ambitious, but I like it.

answers.description: Let's be honest: we're not winning a majority outright. But if we sweep the South and deny both of them 270, this thing goes to the House of Representatives. Then we're the kingmakers.
answers.feedback: Smart. You are focusing on the remaining Southern states to win the region completely.

questions.description: Your campaign has a solid base in the Deep South, but you need to broaden your appeal to shake up this race. Asa Carter has been scouting potential groups that might be receptive to your message. He slides a list across the table. "Governor, we need to pick one of these and go all in. Which one do we chase?

answers.description: We will target war veterans and patriotic societies like the John Birch Society. These folks have been warning about communism for years while the establishment laughed at them. I'll tell them I'm the only candidate who will crush Cienfuegos, win the war in Cuba, and root out every Red sympathizer hiding in our government.
answers.feedback: Most Americans know the John Birch Society from the attempted assassinations of LBJ over the last four years, but this also means you are the only one who can openly appeal to them without restraint.

answers.description: There are millions of folks out there who see their neighborhoods changing, their jobs disappearing, and their country slipping away. While all of this is happening, they are being called racists, nazis and fascists just for demanding to take their country back. We will fight for the America we grew up in.
answers.feedback: So many dog whistles. Your 'people' got the message though, and your vote share in Idaho is increasing for some reason.

answers.description: The faithful are looking for a champion. I'll meet with Billy Graham and every preacher who will have me and I will tell them that I only kneel in front of God himself, and bow to no one else.
answers.feedback: Billy Graham ignored you and compared to Sanders you aren't the most religious man in this race, but this is still a safe way to play.

answers.description: Coming from the coast are millions and millions of aliens who happen to be taking Black jobs. They're taking the employment from Black people. Dear Negroes, my administration will go to work for you as no one has ever done before.
answers.feedback: "The magazine National Review offered a $100 prize to anyone who could identify a Black person who voted for Farris Bryant. Ultimately, very few people managed to claim the prize...."

questions.description: Lyndon Johnson's Great Society has expanded the federal government further than any president since Roosevelt. With Medicare, Medicaid, the promised "War on Poverty", and increased education funding, he's built and building an empire of programs that cost billions and employ thousands of bureaucrats. Now he's running on that record, promising even more if re-elected. Although you promised to dismantle these programs once you reach office, your advisors warn you that many people in the South, including poor whites, depend on them. Will you pivot?

answers.description: I'll tear it down root and branch. Every dime of Johnson's welfare state is a dime stolen from the working man. Medicare was socialism from the start, and the War on Poverty has done nothing but create a class of government dependents.
answers.feedback: This scares many poor people away from your campaign, but you have remained consistent.

answers.description: Some of it stays. Medicare and Social Security could be good. But the rest of it; so the poverty grants, the education mandates, the bureaucrats telling local schools what to teach, that all goes.
answers.feedback: This is a huge pivot. Many conservatives and states' rights activists are mad at you, and are choosing to stay at home or support Sanders instead. However, poor whites and urban workers all across the South are giving your campaign a second look.

answers.description: The Great Society is a perfect example of why Washington should never have been given this much power. I'll send every one of those programs back to the states. If Alabama wants a health program, let Alabama design it.
answers.feedback: Conservatives are pleased, but many voters just hear 'send it back to the states' as 'the programs go away'.

questions.description:
The Republican National Convention was one of the most bitterly divided in memory. Delegates nearly came to blows as conservative Barry Goldwater and liberal Nelson Rockefeller deadlocked ballot after ballot. You emerged as a compromise nominee, but many Goldwater loyalists feel their movement was denied its moment, while Rockefeller supporters worry you'll be a stalking horse for the right. At your first press conference as nominee, a reporter asks:

"Colonel Sanders, how do you intend to unite a party that seems ready to tear itself apart?"

answers.description: Well, I've already sat down with Barry and Nelson and we shook hands like gentlemen. I told them both that I need their ideas, their supporters, and their energy. The Republican Party is a big tent, and my campaign is going to be for everybody; conservatives, liberals, and everyone in between who's fed up with the mess in Washington.
answers.feedback: You are going for the big tent, but this risks dampening base turnout in conservative strongholds.

answers.description: Look, folks, I'm a businessman who believes in limited government, low taxes, and personal responsibility. Barry Goldwater knows that, that's why he agreed to back me. At the same time, I'll show the Rockefeller wing that you can have fiscal discipline and a strong national defense without strangling small businesses in red tape. Common sense unites us, we just have to remember that.
answers.feedback: This will sound conservative to most voters. Let's hope the liberal Republicans won't defect.

answers.description: This is no different than running a franchise operation. You've got different store managers with different ways of doing things, but they all want the same result: a successful restaurant. I'll bring people from all corners of this party into my campaign, and when we win, into my administration. Once folks see we're all working toward the same goal of beating Lyndon Johnson and getting this country back on track, the bickering will seem mighty small.
answers.feedback: You are focusing on your core appeal, but neither wing of the party is excited by this.

questions.description: The Cow Palace is still buzzing after your surprise nomination. Delegates are filing out, reporters are scribbling notes, and your Acceptance Speech is being fervently awaited. What are you telling the crowd?

answers.description: Folks, I spent forty years on the road selling chicken to all kinds of people: Democrats, Republicans, farmers, factory workers, you name it. What I learned is that most folks want the same things: a fair shake, a safe neighborhood, and a government that stays out of their pockets. I intend to talk to everybody exactly like that. You don't have to agree with me on every little thing to know that what we've got right now in Washington ain't working.
answers.feedback: A broad, uplifting appeal that welcomes everyone without watering down your message. It'll play well with independents and disaffected Democrats, but some conservatives may worry you're drifting too far from party orthodoxy.

answers.description: This campaign is for the working families of America. The folks who pack their lunch pails every morning, who scrimp to pay the bills, and who watch their boys get shipped off to die in jungles while Washington fat cats get richer. If they're sick of the chaos, sick of the waste, and sick of a President who's forgotten them, then they've got a home right here.
answers.feedback: A blue-collar, anti-war message that could peel away Johnson's working-class supporters. It might make some conservative Republicans nervous though.

answers.description: Make no mistake, I'm a conservative and I'm proud to be the Republican nominee. When I say this campaign isn't just for Republicans, I mean that we're going to take our principles such as limited government, individual liberty, a strong national defense, and bring them to everyone who shares those values. The door is open. If a Democrat is fed up with Johnson's socialism and his weakness abroad, they're welcome to walk through it.
answers.feedback: This reassures the base that you're one of them, but it's unfortunately not the kind of message that'll bring skeptical Democrats or independents flocking to your banner.

questions.description: You've chosen Maine Senator Margaret Chase Smith as your running mate. Smith is a trailblazer, she is the first woman elected to both houses of Congress and a principled moderate who famously stood up to Joseph McCarthy when her own party was running scared. But some party leaders warn that a woman on the ticket is too bold for the times, especially in the South. Conservative Republicans find her too liberal on civil rights, and even some allies whisper that America isn't ready for a female vice president.

answers.description: Half this country is women, and they've never seen themselves represented at the highest level of government. Margaret Smith has fought for working mothers, for equal pay, for the dignity of every American family. She'll bring millions of voters into this campaign who've been sitting on the sidelines. They say it's risky. I say ignoring half the country is riskier.
answers.feedback: You're making a direct play for women voters, but it's unclear how much Smith will resonate with them.

answers.description: Margaret Smith is respected by Democrats and Republicans alike. She's a moderate who can work across the aisle without abandoning her principles. In a year when this country is divided, I'm picking someone who can bring people together. She'll help me govern from day one, and she'll help me win the independents who decide elections.
answers.feedback: Moderate and statesmanlike, although conservatives are nervous.

questions.description: You've chosen Pennsylvania Governor William Scranton as your running mate. Scranton is young, moderate, and well-regarded but his selection was part of a deal with Nelson Rockefeller, and some Goldwater conservatives are grumbling that you've sold them out.

answers.description: Bill Scranton is a proven leader who's kept the peace in Pennsylvania during some mighty turbulent times. He's got the kind of executive experience you can't learn in a classroom. When we win, he'll be my right-hand man in getting this government running like a well-oiled machine.
answers.feedback: This will play well in the Rust Belt, where his presence on the ticket is already an asset. Goldwater's people will still grumble, but you're not backing down.

answers.description: Governor Scranton and I may come from different wings of the party, but that's exactly the point. We're showing the country that Republicans can work together.
answers.feedback: He'll do fine where you send him to rally, but don't expect him to electrify the base.

questions.description: You've chosen Nebraska Senator Carl Curtis as your running mate. Curtis is a conservative's conservative: a Goldwater ally, a strict constitutionalist, and a man whose states'-rights philosophy resonates with Southern voters who are tired of federal intrusion but uncomfortable with Bryant's extremism. Yet liberal Republicans worry the ticket has abandoned the center entirely. What will you about him?

answers.description: Carl Curtis comes from a little town in Nebraska, and he's never forgotten it. He talks the language of the farmer, the rancher, the working man who feels like Washington stopped listening a long time ago. That's the same language folks speak in Kentucky and Tennessee and a lot of the South. I picked him to send a message to the people who actually grow the food and build the bridges in this country.
answers.feedback: But you are already popular in Nebraska, and it is unclear how appealing he will be to the South.

answers.description: Carl Curtis and I agree on the big things: limited government, fiscal sanity, and a strong national defense. He's a man of his word, which is more than I can say for most of the folks in Washington. When I told the convention I wanted to bring this party together, I meant it. That means I need a running mate our conservative wing can trust. Carl Curtis is that man.
answers.feedback: Some Northern moderates may see Curtis as a step too far right.

questions.description: The front pages this morning carry a shocking report: evidence has emerged that American troops massacred at least 90 unarmed Vietnamese civilians in a village. Coming just days after another rise in casualties, the story has reignited the anti-war movement and put the White House on the defensive.

answers.description: We cannot keep sending our boys into jungles halfway around the world with no plan and no end in sight. I've said it before: if there's no path to peace or victory by January 1968, then we perform an honorable withdrawal by January 1969. That's three years. We beat the Japanese in less time.
answers.feedback: The dovish purists think you're moving too slow, but most Americans just want to know this thing has an end date.

answers.description: Before we talk about strategy, we need to reckon with what just happened. American soldiers killed unarmed civilians, and the President's response has been to circle the wagons. I'll order a full, transparent investigation, and if commanders gave orders that led to this atrocity, they'll be held responsible. America is better than this.
answers.feedback: This is too far to the left for most conservatives, although you have improved your image among doves.

answers.description: The reason we're in this mess is because Lyndon Johnson doubled down on a war he never understood. He ignored his own Secretary of State, he ignored the generals who warned him this would happen, and now innocent people are dead and more American boys are coming home in boxes. Johnson created this disaster. The first thing I'll do is clean house and bring in people who know what they're doing.
answers.feedback: You've put the entire Indochina disaster at Johnson's feet, now some voters think you are too obsessed with the President. This could help Bryant as you and Lyndon attack trade harsh words.

answers.description: I've seen enough. We never should have gone into Indochina in the first place, and we sure as heck shouldn't stay there another day. I'll order our troops home as soon as I take office. Not in three years. Not next Christmas. Now. Let the Vietnamese settle their own affairs. We've spilled enough American blood in somebody else's civil war.
answers.feedback: Hawks in your own party are furious, and Johnson's campaign is already calling you a peacenik who'll abandon America's allies. This is far too dovish, but liberals are flocking to your campaign.

questions.description: You're gathered in a hotel suite with your top advisors: campaign manager Gene Pulliam, spokesman Ron Ziegler, and strategists from the Goldwater and Rockefeller camps. What's the message you're riding on?

answers.description: I've spent my life building a business that employs thousands of people. I know how to balance a budget, I know how to meet a payroll, and I know what it feels like when the government makes that harder instead of easier. This campaign is for the factory workers and the truck drivers, the beauticians and the pipefitters, the small business owners who just want Washington to get off their backs. The Colonel's going to run this country like a successful business and put America back to work.
answers.feedback: A clear, kitchen‑table message that puts your business record front and center. It'll resonate in industrial states that are still hurting from the salad‑oil recession.

answers.description: We're spending blood and treasure in Cuba and Indochina with no end in sight, and the man in the White House keeps telling us victory is just around the corner. I don't want to widen these wars, I want to win them or end them, responsibly. And I know how to organize things to get results. Whether it's a pressure fryer or a foreign policy, you need a steady hand and a clear plan. Johnson has neither. I'll bring both.
answers.feedback: You're taking the fight straight to Johnson on his biggest vulnerability. The anti‑war voters and a lot of exhausted moderates will listen. But you'll need to keep your conservative hawks on board by emphasizing 'win or end it'. If you sound soft, you'll lose the right flank to Bryant.

answers.description: Folks don't trust Washington anymore, and I can't say I blame 'em. I'm not a career politician. I started with nothing, got knocked down more times than I can count, and built something that put food on millions of tables. I'm running to bring that same grit and common sense to the White House.
answers.feedback: Just don't let Johnson's people paint you as an amateur. They'll say the White House isn't a corner diner, and you'd better have an answer.

questions.description: Farris Bryant has taken his segregationist campaign north, drawing big crowds and sparking violent clashes between his supporters and protesters. In Chicago last week, a Bryant rally turned into a street brawl. He is also targeting blue-collar workers which could hurt you. How will you deal with him?

answers.description: Farris Bryant is a sideshow. He's running around hollering about things that ain't never going to happen because he can't win. I've got one opponent in this race worth my time and that's Lyndon Johnson.
answers.feedback: Bryant's base won't grow much if we don't feed him attention. But he could peel off voters we need in border states if we look like we're ducking him.

answers.description: I've seen what happens when you rile folks up with hate, I've stood in front of an angry mob myself down in Sturgis. Bryant is bringing out the worst in people and innocent folks are getting hurt. A man who stirs up that kind of bedlam has no business asking for anybody's vote.
answers.feedback: Taking the high road on law and order. It's what moderates want to hear and it won't cost you any conservative votes that weren't already going to Bryant.

answers.description: Bryant wants to fight the last war. He's living in the past while the rest of us are trying to build a future. I'm for bringing people together, giving every man a fair shot. He's for splitting folks up and turning back the clock. I reckon the voters can tell the difference.
answers.feedback: You sound presidential and forward‑looking. Some of your own supporters might wish you'd hit him harder, but undecided voters will appreciate the grown‑up approach.

answers.description: He's been going around calling me a fake Southerner. Well, I lived in Alabama and Arkansas and I've worked harder jobs than he's ever held. If he wants to compare resumes with a man who's actually built something with his own hands, he's welcome to try. But he might not like what he finds.
answers.feedback: You'll fire up your base and put Bryant on the defensive. But a spat between two Southerners could turn off northern moderates who are tired of the whole mess.

questions.description: President Johnson has declined to participate in a presidential debate. While Bryant had earlier suggest that he would not debate you without Johnson also in attendance, he has since backtracked that notion with the public statement “I look forward to my chat with the Colonel this Monday.” The University of Tennessee was chosen as “neutral ground” between you two. Will you go to debate him?

answers.description: Yes, I will. Bryant wants to keep fighting in Cuba until every last Communist is dead. I want to bring our boys home. I'm going to look him in the eye and ask the mothers of America how many more sons they're willing to lose for his endless war. He talks about total victory like it's a slogan. I've seen what those jungles do to young men.
answers.feedback: The debate was yours, Colonel. You had him sputtering when you asked how many dead soldiers were enough. Polls show voters saw you as the clear winner.

answers.description: Yes, I will. Bryant built his whole campaign on dividing people by the color of their skin. I'm going to remind the country that immigrant and colored folks are just like us lifelong Americans; they’re studious, industrious, ambitious and hard-working dreamers and democracy-lovers. A man who stirs up hate to win votes doesn't deserve to hold any office in this land.
answers.feedback: The debate was yours, Colonel. You made him look small and stuck in the past. Civil rights voters are taking notice, and northern moderates are impressed.

answers.description: Yes, I will. Bryant talks big about helping working folks, but his whole platform is about fighting and dividing. I'm going to ask him what he's going to do for the factory worker who got laid off, or the farmer who can't get a fair price. He's got no answer because he's never run a business or met a payroll.
answers.feedback: The debate was yours, Colonel. Bryant had no answer on pocketbook issues and looked out of his depth.

answers.description: I've already said my piece. Bryant is just looking for attention and I'm not going to give it to him. He's a third-party candidate with no path to victory. The voters know where I stand, and I'd rather spend my time talking to folks directly than sharing a stage with a man who peddles in hate.
answers.feedback: Skipping the debate keeps Bryant from getting the spotlight, but some voters wonder if you're afraid of him.

questions.description: You're in Dothan, Alabama, shaking hands after a speech when a man charges at you with a knife. You swing your cane and knock the blade out of his hand before striking him in the jaw. The attacker is in custody, and you're unharmed, thank God.

answers.description: I didn't have time to think. I just saw the knife and my cane was already in my hand, so I used it. I've been in tight spots before and I reckon I've still got some fight left in me. A man tries to harm me over my beliefs, well, he's going to find out I don't rattle easy.
answers.feedback:
Colonel, the whole country just saw a 74-year-old man disarm a would-be killer with nothing but a walking cane.

SANDERS LEADING JOHNSON BY 10% IN LATEST POLLS

– The Washington Post, 9/7/1964

questions.description: Happy Chandler, your old rival from Kentucky, has been stumping for President Johnson across the South. At a rally in St. Louis, he told the crowd that your hometown of Corbin once ran out its entire Negro population, that you've never truly supported integration, and that "under a Colonel Presidency, we can kiss Civil Rights goodbye." How will you answer?

answers.description: I didn't live in Corbin when that ugly business happened back in 1919, and I never would have supported it. Anybody who knows me knows I've always treated folks equally. I marched with Dr. King.  My company hires based on the content of your work, not the color of your skin. Happy Chandler is just sore because I beat him fair and square back in '55 and he's never gotten over it.
answers.feedback: Civil rights leaders are cheering, but you've probably lost any chance of winning over southern whites who were on the fence. Bryant will call you a radical.

answers.description: I believe every American deserves a fair shake. That's why I've always hired people based on their abilities and treated every customer the same. But I also believe you can't force folks to change overnight with a stack of federal papers. A lot of these decisions are best made by communities and states, not by Washington bureaucrats. I haven't even read the whole Civil Rights Act yet. When I'm President, I'll take a good look at it, and if any part of it does more harm than good, off it'll go.
answers.feedback: This is a big change from your previous position. Southerners will like this, but a lot of northern liberals are shocked.

answers.description: What I care about right now is stopping the riots and the violence that are tearing this country apart. Black folks and white folks are both suffering from the chaos in our streets. I'm going to restore order, and when things are calm, we can work through these problems neighbor to neighbor. That's the kind of leadership that's been missing. Chandler can sling mud all he wants. I'm focused on keeping Americans safe.
answers.feedback: Moderates who are scared of the riots will nod along, but civil rights supporters will notice you didn't actually defend your record, and they might start wondering whose side you're really on.

questions.description: Although your anti-war views are widely supported, many people still question your wartime credentials. Your advisers are recommending that you take a tour abroad to demonstrate your statesmanship.

answers.description: I wanted to show those folks that America is still open for business. We talked about the chicken tariff mess, about how trade wars hurt everybody; farmers, factory workers, families on both sides of the ocean. I've been doing business across borders for years, and I told them a Sanders administration will tear down those walls and get commerce flowing again. A strong economy is the best foreign policy there is.
answers.feedback: You framed the whole trip around jobs and trade, which plays to your strongest suit. With that said, LBJ is still seen as the more experienced candidate.

answers.description: I went over there to listen. The world is a dangerous place right now, and our allies are worried. They wanted to know if America is still going to stand by them. I told them yes, but also that we can't be the world's policeman forever. We need strong allies who can pull their own weight. I learned that these leaders are hungry for steady, honest American leadership. I intend to give it to them.
answers.feedback: Hawkish voters are a little uneasy about the 'not the world's policeman' line, but allies and anti-war voters appreciate the restraint. With that said, LBJ is still seen as the more experienced candidate.

answers.description: I told them I was there to learn, not to lecture. I've never pretended to be some big-shot diplomat. But you don't build a worldwide business without knowing how to sit down with folks, listen to their problems, and find common ground. I asked a lot of questions. I found out that our friends in Europe respect strength, but they're tired of being talked down to. A little humility goes a long way.
answers.feedback: You came off humble and honest. That's refreshing, and it's very you. Just be ready for Johnson to call it a 'sightseeing tour.'

questions.description: A man from Tennessee has gone to the tabloids claiming you stole the 11 herbs and spices recipe from him back in 1949. The story is spreading, and reporters are shouting questions at your next campaign stop.

answers.description: This smells like a dirty trick from somebody who doesn't want me in the White House. I don't know if it's Johnson's people or Bryant's, but somebody put this man up to it. They're getting desperate because our polls are climbing. I've got nothing to hide, and when the truth comes out, the folks who cooked up this nonsense are going to have a lot of explaining to do.
answers.feedback: This sounds overly negative to most voters, and you advisors sigh.

answers.description: That's a bald-faced lie. I created that recipe in my own kitchen way back in 1939, years before I ever met this fella. Hundreds of people ate my chicken at the Sanders Court and Café and they'll tell you it tastes exactly the same today as it did then. We've already got lawyers drawing up papers for slander. You don't get to smear a man's life work with a tall tale and just walk away.
answers.feedback: The evidence piled up: hundreds of people stepped forward swearing the recipe never changed, and that Tennessee fella admitted he made the whole thing up. You'll still get a bit hurt though.

answers.description: I've got franchisees all over this country who've been making my chicken for years. Not one of them has ever come forward and said the recipe changed or that it wasn't mine. I'll let my customers and my workers speak for me. They know the truth. This fella can say whatever he wants, but a good product speaks for itself.
answers.feedback: A quieter approach, this will give your opponents lots of space to attack you. At least you didn't fall into the gutter.

questions.description: You’ve spent the past few days campaigning through the South, and your staff is divided. Some say you need to emphasize your Kentucky roots and time in Alabama and Arkansas to win over conservative whites. Others warn that leaning too hard into that image will cost you the northern moderates who are just starting to give you a look.

answers.description: I’ve lived in Alabama, I practiced law in Arkansas, and I spent years working on the railroads through these mountains. I know these people because I am these people. I’m a conservative who believes in hard work, limited government, and the Constitution. Folks down here want a President who understands their way of life instead of some Washington politician who talks down to them, and I aim to give them that.
answers.feedback: You’re doubling down on your Southern credentials, and conservative whites down here are taking notice. Bryant can’t call you a Yankee anymore. But some of your moderate supporters up north are getting skittish.

answers.description: Kentucky sits right between North and South, and I think that’s an advantage. I understand both sides of this country’s arguments because I’ve lived with one foot in each world. I don’t pander to extremists on either end. I’m going to talk to Southern voters the same way I talk to folks in Ohio and Pennsylvania: straight, honest, and respectful. Most folks, wherever they live, just want a fair shake.
answers.feedback: This is a refreshing message that plays well in border states and suburbs, but Bryant will keep attacking you.

answers.description: I’m not running to be President of the South or President of the North. I’m running to be President of all Americans. What unites a farmer in Georgia and a steelworker in Indiana is the same thing: a government that’s taken too much of their money and given back too little. I’ll talk about jobs, wages, and getting Washington off your back. That’s a message that works everywhere.
answers.feedback: Just be careful: Many of the swing states are in the south.

questions.description: "Cam bomb", the explosive device set by Communist guerrillas loyal to Camilo Cienfuegos, the leader still fighting American forces in Cuba, has detonated in the U.S. embassy in Havana, seriously wounding the ambassador. Meanwhile, thousands of Cuban refugees continue to arrive on Florida's shores, fleeing the war, stoking fears that such bombings could happen on U.S. soil, too. Governor Bryant is blaming both you and Johnson for the chaos and calling for mass deportations. How will you respond?

answers.description: First thing, we seal off any gaps in our security and make sure these bombers can't slip through. I'll order the FBI and every federal agency to hunt down anyone connected to Cienfuegos and bring them to justice. Refugees are welcome if they're peaceful and law-abiding, but anybody who comes here to do us harm will find no safe harbor.
answers.feedback: A straightforward law-and-order answer. Voters scared about the bombings will feel reassured, but you are seen as too soft on immigration across the south.

answers.description: The reason we have Cam bombs going off in Cuba is because Lyndon Johnson can't bring himself to either win this war or end it. He keeps our boys over there in a stalemate, and now the fighting has spilled into the cities. I'll bring our troops home on a real timetable and stop playing games with American lives.
answers.feedback: Some moderates may worry you're using a tragedy for attacking Johnson only, but he is so unpopular that this might work.

answers.description: These folks fleeing Cuba are running from the same Communists we're fighting. They're looking for freedom, not trouble. I'll set up a fair system to welcome them in while making darn sure we vet every single one. And those Cam bombers? They're murderers. They'll face the full weight of the law.
answers.feedback: This will completely kill your ratings in the south, but at least your protected your compassionate image.

answers.description: If Cienfuegos wants to send his bombers into our neighborhoods, then he ought to know I've still got my pressure fryer and a fresh batch of secret herbs and spices! I'll fly down to Havana myself, grab that varmint by the collar, and personally escort him to a courtroom. Then maybe I'll sit him down and make him eat a bucket of KFC so he can see what a free country tastes like.
answers.feedback: ....what?

questions.description: Labor unions have traditionally been a Democratic stronghold, and President Johnson has secured the endorsements of nearly every major union. Yet your crowds are full of factory workers, truck drivers, and miners. Farris Bryant is also barnstorming the industrial towns, telling working-class whites that both you and Johnson have abandoned them. What will be your strategy for working-class voters?

answers.description: I never finished the seventh grade. I've shoveled coal, laid railroad ties, painted barns, and sold insurance door to door. I know what it's like to wake up sore and wonder if you've got enough to get by. I didn't inherit a dime. Everything I built, I built with my own two hands. So when I talk about making this country work for working people, I'm not reading off some speechwriter's notes. I've lived it.
answers.feedback: Nobody can out-work your life story. When you talk about shoveling coal, these folks see one of their own. The union leadership is still with Johnson, but the rank and file are starting to drift our way. Also the mention of coal makes you even more popular in West Virginia. But recent endorsements also gave LBJ a boost.

answers.description: Lyndon Johnson likes to wrap himself in the union label, but this is the same man who voted for the Taft-Hartley Act. He talks big about standing with workers, then turns around and signs bills that ship jobs overseas. Union bosses might be in his pocket, but rank-and-file workers know the truth. I'll be a President who actually fights for American jobs instead of just posing for pictures at the union hall.
answers.feedback: Taft-Hartley is a dirty word in union halls, and reminding folks he voted for it really stings. The union bosses won't flip, but the workers are listening. On the other hand, GOP elites are confused. Bryant attacks you for threatening to destroy right-to-work laws.

answers.description: The best thing you can do for a working man is make sure he has a steady job that pays a decent wage. I've created thousands of jobs through my company, and I pay folks enough that they don't need tips to get by. I'll bring that same philosophy to Washington: cut the red tape that strangles small businesses, keep factories here instead of overseas, and make sure a hard day's work earns a fair day's pay.
answers.feedback: You're staying positive and forward-looking. It's not the most fiery message, and recent endorsements also gave LBJ a boost.

answers.description: Farris Bryant comes to your town and talks a good game, but all he really cares about is stirring up anger and splitting folks apart. You can't build a strong economy on hate. While he's pitting white workers against black workers, the big corporations are laughing all the way to the bank. I'll unite working people around what they have in common: the need for good jobs, safe streets, and a government that doesn't treat them like fools.
answers.feedback: This is a harsh attack against Bryant which could help you pull away northern voters from him, but LBJ remains above the bickering and omes across as the winner.

questions.description: President Johnson has been touring retirement communities and senior centers, touting the Medicare and Medicaid programs he signed into law. His campaign is running ads claiming that you'd roll back these benefits and leave the elderly out in the cold. How will you respond?

answers.description: Lyndon Johnson can promise you the moon, but here's the problem: his spending is driving up prices so fast that your benefits are worth less every month. He's printing money, running up the debt, and your Social Security check doesn't go as far as it used to. I'll stop the wasteful spending and protect the value of what you've earned. A dollar in your pocket is worth more than a promise from a politician.
answers.feedback: Is Goldwater speaking through you? This is a sensitive issue for many voters, especially the elderly, and it confirms their concerns about you.

answers.description: I've spent years working with Jerry Lewis to raise money for the Muscular Dystrophy Association. Private citizens, churches, and community groups can do a lot of good without the government getting in the middle. I'll make sure there's a safety net for folks who truly need it, but I also believe the best help comes from your neighbors, not a bureaucrat in Washington.
answers.feedback: This is far too conservative for the most.

answers.description: I'm not going to take away your healthcare. What I will do is make sure these programs aren't wasting your tax dollars on bureaucracy and paperwork. I've run a business that serves millions of people without drowning in red tape. The government ought to be able to do the same. You paid into these programs. You deserve them to work right.
answers.feedback: This won't stop the attacks, but at least you sound moderate. Bryant will instantly claim that you are completely behind the Great Society, framing you as being no different to LBJ unfortunately.

questions.description: Governor George Wallace of Alabama, a Democrat who broke with the segregationists and now supports integration, has been campaigning hard for President Johnson across the South. He's telling voters that Johnson is the only candidate who can be trusted on civil rights while also understanding the South. All 3 candidates seem to be have a chance to potentially win the south, what will you do?

answers.description: Governor Wallace is strong on civil rights, and I give him credit for that. But with all due respect, he's backing the wrong horse. Lyndon Johnson has been in Washington for thirty years, and what's the South got to show for it? Poverty, job losses, and boys dying in Cuba. I'll bring something Johnson can't: a businessman who'll put the South back to work.
answers.feedback: You deliver your usual message while LBJ gains ground in the south.

answers.description: I'm not going to say a bad word about George Wallace. He's doing what he thinks is right. But plenty of folks who voted for him are looking for something different this time. My door is open. If you believe in law and order, good jobs, and a government that leaves you alone, you've got a home in this campaign, whether you're a Democrat or a Republican, black or white.
answers.feedback: This is a neutral response. Wallace appreciates your words and promises future cooperation regardless of the outcome of the election. The only problem is that embracing integrationist Wallace disappoints the few supporters who expected a more conservative position.

answers.description: George Wallace isn't on the ballot. Lyndon Johnson is. Wallace can stump for whoever he wants, but I'm running against the President, not the Governor of Alabama. Folks in the South are smart enough to make up their own minds without being told what to do by a politician from Montgomery.
answers.feedback: Most southerners (at least the ones who aren't die-hard segregationists) trusts Wallace more than you. This will help LBJ.

questions.description: The “Shoutnik” movement is a group of young anti-war activists who burn draft cards, march on college campuses, and openly mock traditional values, and they have become a flashpoint in the campaign. President Johnson calls them a nuisance, Bryant wants them arrested and you have the same opinion, but now your own daughter Margaret has urged you to be more understanding. Have you changed your position?

answers.description: I don’t drink, I don’t smoke, and I believe in old-fashioned hard work. That’s who I am, and I’m too old to pretend otherwise. But I also raised a daughter who’s dragged me to more protests than I can count, and I’ve learned you don’t have to agree with someone to listen to them. These young folks want peace and fairness. I disagree with their methods, but not their goals. I’ll be a President who respects their passion even when I don’t share their lifestyle.
answers.feedback: Bryant is having a field day with your words, even LBJ is criticising your alleged soft attitude towards shoutniks, but young people are listening.

answers.description: I make no apologies for the way I live. I built a successful business without touching a drop of liquor or chasing every new fad that comes along. This country doesn't need a shoutnik, it needs one who knows the difference between right and wrong and isn’t afraid to say so. Young people will figure that out when they grow up, just like every generation before them.
answers.feedback: The churchgoers and country-club Republicans are cheering, but good luck rallying in the west coast from now on.

answers.description: Farris Bryant sends his followers into the streets to beat up protesters. Lyndon Johnson sends in the National Guard and then hides from the consequences. I’m the only candidate who’s actually sat down and talked to these young folks and to their worried parents. The problem is leaders who don’t know how to keep the peace without cracking skulls, not the kids.
answers.feedback: People are wondering if you can ever answer a question without mentioning the other candidates. Also, these words are too soft on shoutniks.

questions.description: The economy is still reeling from the “Salad Oil Recession”: A New Jersey commodities trader named Tino De Angelis swindled banks and brokers out of nearly $175 million by pretending to own vast tanks of soybean oil that were mostly seawater. When the scheme collapsed last November, it brought down brokerage firms, froze credit, and sent the stock market into a tailspin. Unemployment is up, small businesses can't get loans, and President Johnson's response has been widely criticized as slow and inadequate. What will you do about it?

answers.description: The first thing I'll do is tell every federal agency to stop strangling small businesses with paperwork. I've dealt with these regulators myself, they'd rather fill out forms than let a man run his shop. Second, I'll push for a temporary tax cut on new hires so businesses can start putting people back to work. Confidence is like a campfire: you've got to nurse it back slowly, and the government's job is to stop stomping on the kindling.
answers.feedback: Johnson's people will say you're just recycling old Republican talking points, but your economic credentials are trusted.

answers.description: The little guy always pays the price while the big shots skate away. De Angelis swindled billions, and the banks that looked the other way are still doing business as usual. I'll order a full investigation into exactly how this happened and who let it happen. Then I'll make sure the rules get rewritten so no single con man can wreck the whole economy again. Honest businessmen have nothing to fear from that.
answers.feedback: This is a populist response that will anger your donors and the conservatives. Let's see if the working-class voters can make up for it.

answers.description: Every time Washington tries to fix a problem, it makes it worse. Johnson threw money at this recession and all we got was more debt and more inflation. The economy knows how to heal itself if the government stops interfering. I'll cut spending, balance the budget, and let honest businessmen and workers do what they do best without some bureaucrat second-guessing them.
answers.feedback: This is what the conservative base wants to hear. 'Let the market fix itself' sounds good in theory, but folks without jobs want action.

questions.description: President Johnson has been crisscrossing the country with a simple message: "It is best to not switch horses in mid‑stream." He argues that with wars in Cuba and Indochina, economic uncertainty, and civil unrest, this is no time to hand the White House to an inexperienced outsider. A reporter asks for your response.

answers.description: You do if your horse is drowning! Johnson's been in the saddle for four years, and look at the mess we're in. Our boys are dying in two wars with no end in sight. Bombs are going off in Florida. The economy is in the ditch. If this is what staying the course looks like, I think the American people are ready to swim for shore.
answers.feedback: That line about the drowning horse is going in every newspaper tomorrow. He handed you that opening, and you rode it right through.

answers.description: The President says don't change horses. I say when the rider has been riding you straight into a swamp, it's time to find a new rider. I've spent my whole life pulling myself out of tough spots and building something from nothing. I didn't get here by sticking with a losing hand, and neither should the American people.
answers.feedback: You emphasize your past as usual.

questions.description: American soldiers are still dying in the jungles of Cuba and along the Laos-Vietnam border, years after both conflicts began. Cam bombs have hit American soil, the Indochina casualty lists grow longer every week, and President Johnson's approval on foreign policy has cratered. Your poll ratings keep increasing as we come closer to the election day.

answers.description: I've said it before: if we can't win this thing in three years, we bring our boys home. No more open-ended commitments, no more sending soldiers to die without a plan. I'll give the commanders a real chance to finish the job, but the days of endless war stop the moment I take office.
answers.feedback: This is popular with most people expect the few hawks.

questions.description: At a rally in South Carolina, a local Republican leader introduces you with faint praise, then privately warns your campaign that many southern conservatives are uneasy. "The Colonel says government ought to leave folks alone," he tells an aide, "but down here we expect a president to stand up for Christian values. We don't want Washington telling us what to do on race, but we sure want it to keep the country from sliding into moral decay." What do you think?

answers.description: I've never needed the government to tell me how to live a decent life. I don't drink, I don't smoke, I don't chase women, and I go to church on Sunday. That's between me and the Lord, not me and some bureaucrat. I trust folks to raise their families right without Washington butting in. That's real conservatism, not the kind that wants a policeman in every pulpit.
answers.feedback: Libertarians love it, but religious conservatives distrust you.

answers.description: I believe in leading by example, not by force. You want a president who lives by the values this country was built on? Look at my life. But I'm not going to use federal agents to make people behave. That's how they do things in Moscow. Freedom means you get to choose right from wrong, and most folks, given the chance, will choose right.
answers.feedback: You are trying to highlight your character without sounding preachy, but criticisms keep coming.

answers.description: This country was built on certain eternal truths: faith, family, hard work, and personal responsibility. I'm not ashamed to say that a President ought to stand up for those things. I'll protect the right to worship, I'll stand against the smut peddlers who want to corrupt our children, and I'll make sure Washington never tramples on the moral convictions of decent Americans. If that makes me old-fashioned, so be it.
answers.feedback: Southern conservatives and evangelicals are thrilled as the Bryant campaign just lost one of its best arguments. But libertarian Republicans and northern suburbanites are getting nervous, they didn't sign up for a culture crusade.

questions.description: The phrase "Lying Lyndon" started in conservative circles but has spread far beyond them. President Johnson promised the Cuban War would be over by Christmas 1963. It wasn't. He promised no wider war in Indochina. Then he doubled the troop commitment. He said the economy was sound. Then the salad oil scandal sent it spiraling. Even some Democrats quietly admit the President has a credibility problem. What is your opinion?

answers.description: The President told the country we'd be out of Cuba by last Christmas. Then this Christmas. Now nobody knows. He told Congress he wasn't expanding the war in Indochina, then sent thousands more troops. At some point you have to ask: does he know what he's doing, or is he just saying whatever it takes to get through the week? I'll never make a promise I can't keep.
answers.feedback: The base is fired up. Some swing voters might think it's a little harsh, but nobody can say you're wrong.

answers.description: The problem is bigger than one man. Washington is full of folks who'll tell you one thing to your face and do another behind closed doors. I've spent my life in business where a handshake means something. If I'm elected, I'll bring that same standard to the White House. No double-talk, no hidden agendas. The American people deserve a government as honest as they are.
answers.feedback: This taps into the anti-Washington sentiment that's driving this election, and it makes you look like the outsider who'll clean house.

questions.description: In June, President Johnson issued an executive order ending graduate school deferments, meaning college students who once avoided conscription now face the draft. Campus protests have erupted, and many young voters who supported Johnson in 1960 are now flocking to your rallies. What will you say about the draft?

answers.description: I don't believe in special treatment for anybody, rich or poor, college or no college. If we're going to have a draft, it ought to be fair. But I'll tell you what I told my own grandson: serving your country is an honor. What's wrong right now is that we're asking young men to die in wars with no clear purpose. I'll give our commanders a real plan, and if the wars aren't won or settled in three years, we bring everyone home. That's how you make the draft less of a tragedy.
answers.feedback: While this is more in line with the national position, the young people who are supporting your campaign are feeling a little disappointed.

answers.description: I'll reinstate those deferments on day one. Young people pursuing an education aren't draft dodgers, they're building their futures and this country's future. Johnson punished them for speaking out against his failures. I'll listen to them instead. And I'll work to end these wars so the question of who gets drafted stops being a matter of life and death.
answers.feedback: The campuses are going to explode with support, but older voters and veterans might see it as coddling draft dodgers. Johnson will call you soft, and Bryant will say you're undermining the war effort.

questions.description: Months ago, Malcolm X’s five‑year‑old daughter was shot in a drive‑by attack. Malcolm responded by killing Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan, then surrendered peacefully. In the aftermath, a group of young black activists formed a vigilante group called the X‑Men, vowing to protect black communities by any means necessary. Race riots have shaken cities across the North and Midwest. Civil rights leaders are divided. Will you condemn this group?

answers.description: I don’t care who you are or what cause you claim to serve. When private citizens take up arms and appoint themselves judge and jury, you’ve got anarchy. I’ll enforce the law equally against every vigilante group, white or black. Justice doesn't come from a gang with guns.
answers.feedback: Law‑and‑order voters and suburban whites will applaud, but civil rights leaders are already calling your statement tone‑deaf.

answers.description: I’ve sat with Dr. King. I’ve marched with folks who’ve been beaten and hosed for asking to be treated like human beings. I understand why some young black men feel the law has failed them. But armed vigilantes will only make things worse. I’ll protect every American’s rights, and I’ll enforce the law fairly. You can’t heal a wound by cutting it deeper.
answers.feedback: This is a careful balance, but you sound too mild for a lot of conservatives.

answers.description: Malcolm X’s little girl was shot by cowards, and the police did nothing. I can’t fault a man for wanting to protect his family. The Constitution gives Americans the right to bear arms for their own defense. I won’t let Washington disarm law‑abiding citizens who are just trying to keep their children safe.
answers.feedback: This is a high‑stakes gamble, Colonel. Black Americans are embracing you, but your core supporters are shocked that you seem content with a group of armed black vigilantes.

questions.description: President Johnson has now survived two attempts on his life: first in 1962 by a Klansman, then in 1963 by a former Marine with John Birch Society ties. He's pushing Congress for new gun laws: restrictions on mail‑order weapons, tighter background checks, and federal oversight of interstate firearm sales. Conservatives in both parties are resisting, and Second Amendment groups are mobilizing. Everyone is curious about your position.

answers.description: The Second Amendment isn't a suggestion. It's the right of every law‑abiding American to protect themselves and their families. I've been in tight spots where a firearm saved my life and the lives of others. Criminals don't follow gun laws. They never have. I'm not going to punish honest citizens for the acts of madmen.
answers.feedback: After two presidential assassination attempts, some suburban voters are going to see this as callous. You might sound like you care more about guns than about a President nearly dying.

answers.description: Both men who tried to kill the President were deeply disturbed ex‑Marines with known mental problems. The failure wasn't with the gun laws; it was with a system that let those men slip through the cracks. I'll double funding for veterans' mental health and make sure the states actually report dangerous individuals. Treat the sickness instead of the symptom.
answers.feedback: Mental health is a real problem, and you're offering a genuine solution. However, LBJ says the same thing, so your words don't gain any traction.

answers.description: I'm a businessman, and I believe in common sense. There's no reason a man should be able to order a rifle through the mail without anybody checking who he is. I'll back a law that stops interstate sales to criminals and the dangerously insane while protecting the rights of honest sportsmen and families.
answers.feedback: This aligns with the views of the average American.

questions.description: Your running mate, Governor William Scranton of Pennsylvania, is taking heat from all sides. Bryant's campaign calls him a "Rockefeller puppet" who'll drag you left on spending and civil rights. Johnson's surrogates say Scranton lacks foreign policy experience and isn't ready to step into the presidency. Even some Goldwater Republicans quietly grumble that he's too moderate. How will you defend your ticket?

answers.description: Bill Scranton kept the peace in Pennsylvania when other states were burning. He balanced a budget, he managed a state bigger than most countries, and he did it without the corrupt machine politics that Johnson and his crew depend on. Anybody who says he's not ready for the job hasn't been paying attention. I picked him because he's exactly the kind of steady, principled leader this country needs.
answers.feedback: Scranton's team is grateful, and voters in Pennsylvania are taking notice. But you've tied yourself more closely to a moderate, which might cool enthusiasm among some Goldwater conservatives who were already suspicious of him.

answers.description: Bill Scranton doesn't need me to fight his battles for him. He's a grown man who's been taking hits from Democrats and winning elections in a tough state for years. I'll let him speak for himself, and I think folks are going to like what they hear.
answers.feedback: Scranton feels a bit disapointed, but it will likely not be a big issue in this election.

questions.description: Your running mate, Senator Carl Curtis, is under fire. Johnson's campaign is circulating a clip from a small-town rally where Curtis, responding to a question about government spending, said: "I carried my own lunch to school as a youth... and it built my character. We are destroying the moral fiber of our youth by feeding them for free" Johnson's surrogates have seized on the remark and even some of your own staff are urging you to distance yourself.

answers.description: Now, I've told him he could have put that a whole lot better, and he knows it. But I've put my foot in my mouth more times than I can count, and I'm not going to hang a good man out to dry over one clumsy sentence.
answers.feedback: Curtis is glad that you are backing him, although the President accuse you of being just another Goldwater..

answers.description: This is what the other side does when they can't defend their own record. They find one sentence, strip it of all context, and try to make the whole campaign about it. Voters are smart enough to see through these cheap tricks, and they're smart enough to know when somebody's trying to distract them from the real issues.
answers.feedback: It's good to be aggressive, but unfortunately LBJ is much better at that.

questions.description: Your running mate, Senator Margaret Chase Smith, is under fire. Bryant has called her a "Yankee feminist who wants to wreck the American family." Even some Republican congressmen privately grumble that her refusal to campaign modernly by not attending rallies is a gift to the opposition. How do you respond?

answers.description: These fellas are scared. They're scared of a woman who's smarter than they are and braver than they'll ever be. Bryant calls her a Yankee feminist because he can't imagine a woman who thinks for herself. Margaret Smith is no radical. She's a patriot who's given her life to this country. Anyone suggesting otherwise is just trying to distract you from the real issues.
answers.feedback: Bold statements, but they sounds too obnoxious for the average American.

answers.description: I didn't pick Margaret Smith to make a statement. I picked her because she knows how to get things done. She's passed major legislation, she's commanded respect from both parties, and she'll be ready to step in on day one if anything happens to me. All this talk about her being a radical, that's just noise. What matters is whether she can do the job, and I've got no doubt she can.
answers.feedback: Attacks continue.

questions.description:
It's the last week of the campaign. Your campaign plane is fueled and ready, but there's only time for one more intensive swing through a key region. Your advisors are gathered around a map in a hotel suite. Gene Pulliam speaks first:

"Colonel, we can't be everywhere. Where are we going to spend these final days?"

answers.description: The Deep South. Bryant thinks he's got these folks locked up. I aim to show them there's a conservative on the ballot who isn't running on hate. I'll campaign on jobs, law and order, and my time living in Alabama and Arkansas. Some of these states are closer than they look, and I've never been afraid of a long shot.
answers.feedback: Ambitious. If we crack the Solid South, we reshape American politics.

answers.description: The Northwest. These voters are sick of war and they don't trust Johnson. I'll talk about my plan to bring the boys home, about restoring honesty to government. Oregon went for Morse in the primaries, and Washington's been flirting with Republicans lately. We could pick up a couple of states there.
answers.feedback: The anti‑war vote is strong here and our message resonates. But these states are small in electoral weight. If we lose Pennsylvania or Ohio chasing Oregon, we'll regret it.

answers.description: The Border states and Upper South. This is where elections are won. These states know me, they're full of folks like me, and they're up for grabs. I'll remind Arkansas I practiced law there, remind Tennessee I respect their values, and remind Virginia I'm a business man, not a Washington bureaucrat. Win here and the Electoral College falls into place.
answers.feedback: Smart, safe, and essential. These are the swing states we need to win, and we're competitive in every one.

answers.description: The Midwest and Mid‑Atlantic. The industrial heartland decides this election. We can lock down Pennsylvania, and West Virginia's miners are listening to us. Ohio's always a bellwether. We pour everything into the big electoral prizes and let the rest of the map take care of itself.
answers.feedback: The heavyweights. Pennsylvania alone is a monster prize, and Ohio and West Virginia are pivotal.

scenarioDescription:
Read the original scenario by gap80 here: https://www.alternatehistory.com/forum/threads/kentucky-fried-politics-a-colonel-sanders-timeline.516244/

Colonel Harland Sanders, the fried chicken tycoon and former Governor of Kentucky, leads the Republican ticket against incumbent President Lyndon B. Johnson and third-party challenger Farris Bryant. America is reeling from a bloody stalemate in Cuba, an expanding war in Indochina, and the economic fallout of a massive "salad oil" recession. Johnson, once a master legislator, now faces deep unpopularity after a bitter primary fight and escalating riots at home. Sanders, a folksy moderate with a strong civil rights record, emerged as a compromise nominee from a deadlocked GOP convention. Bryant's segregationist Heritage Independence Party threatens to peel away Southern states by vowing to restore "traditional values" and crush communism with overwhelming force.

How will their campaigns unfold? Can Sanders overcome an incumbent in wartime? Will Johnson salvage his Great Society, or will the White House change hands?
